metaDescription: Six fruit picker poles compared by length, locking system and material, from short sectional shafts to 26 foot telescoping poles for tall fruit trees.
introParagraphs: The pole is the part of a fruit picker that decides whether harvest day is pleasant or exhausting. A good pole extends smoothly, locks without a fight, stays straight when a basket full of fruit loads the tip, and does not slip when the sap and dew get involved. A poor one sags, wobbles or collapses a section at the wrong moment. This guide ranks six picker poles by how they are built and how they behave, and each comes with a catch basket attached. Think of the shaft as the engine of the tool and the basket as only the final inch.

Two construction styles dominate. The SKGPOLE, TONYINGO and LAANPOLE poles are 26 foot telescoping designs that extend in one motion and lock at preset heights. The Walensee 13FT and BlumeTrec 6.5FT use stainless steel sections, and the ALongwujin uses interchangeable segments you add or remove. Each style trades off speed, weight and reach, and we explain the differences in plain language. That variety means there is a sensible pole for a patio lemon tree as well as for a mature orchard apple.

We evaluated every pick from its listing specs and buyer feedback, and lengths and materials are the makers' claims. The most important note comes first: a metal pole near overhead power lines is a serious hazard, so the best pole for you is the shortest one that reaches your fruit from firm, level ground. With those points in mind, the sections below walk through each pole and then through the main decisions.

products.name: TONYINGO 26FT Reach Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The TONYINGO 26FT is built around preset heights. The telescoping pole locks at 5, 9, 12, 16 and 20 feet, so you extend it to one of five known lengths rather than guessing. The listing stresses that there is no tedious assembly, and the large metal basket measures 5.7 by 13 inches, which is longer and deeper than most heads on the market.

Preset stops make the pole predictable. If you know your tree needs the 12 foot stop, you can set it there every time. For someone who would rather not fiddle with sections, that repeatability is a real comfort, and it helps you teach a family member how to use it.

The cost is that five stops will not fit every branch exactly, so you sometimes pick between two lengths. Aluminum is typical of poles in this class, and it conducts electricity, so keep it far from lines. Compared with the SKGPOLE, the TONYINGO has more defined stops and a larger basket. It is the best fit for people who value simple, repeatable setup. Extend it on the ground first and count the stops against the height of your tree, so you know which stop you will use most. When you finish for the day, collapse it fully from the top section down and let it air dry. The wide basket is also forgiving when your aim is a little off, which counts for a lot at 16 feet.
products.bestFor: People who want predictable preset lengths and a large basket.
pros: Reach up to 26 feet by the maker's claim
cons: Metal pole near wires is dangerous

products.name: SKGPOLE 26FT Reach Fruit Picker Extension Pole
products.description:
The SKGPOLE gives you a high-quality extension pole with a thread that matches the market. Its aluminum shaft telescopes from 5 to 20 feet, the maker states reach of up to 26 feet, and the 3/4 inch American standard thread means other compatible heads can be swapped on if you ever need one. The included metal basket is 5.5 inches across with a thick foam pad.

Using a standard thread is a quiet advantage. You can fit a different head, a pruner, or another threaded accessory to the same pole. That makes the SKGPOLE the most flexible pole in the group for a gardener who owns other tools.

The listing describes the pole as sturdy and made of high-quality aluminum that will not break easily. As with other telescoping poles, keep the sections clean and wipe off sap. Compared with the TONYINGO, the SKGPOLE has a smaller basket but a thread you can reuse. It is a good everyday tall pole. If you already own a threaded paint pole or a pruner head, check whether it fits this shaft before buying a second pole. Keep the thread clean with a dry cloth and avoid cross-threading when you screw a head on. Owners who also keep a pruning head for the same thread can use one pole for both jobs across the year.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who want a tall pole that fits standard threaded tools.
pros: Reach up to 26 feet by the maker's claim
Thick foam pad in the basket
cons: Basket is smaller than the TONYINGO

products.name: LAANPOLE 26FT Reach Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The LAANPOLE offers the same 5 to 20 foot telescoping range as its rivals, with a maker-stated reach of over 26 feet and a bowl-shaped foam cushion at the bottom of the basket. The listing describes a stable and relatively lightweight build and says the cushion guarantees a soft landing for picked fruit.

The bowl shape is the notable detail. A cushion that curves up the sides holds fruit in the middle of the basket, rather than letting it roll against the wire. That keeps fruit from bumping each other as you lower the pole.

Because the listing gives fewer technical details than the SKGPOLE, test the locks early and make sure the sections hold. Compared with the TONYINGO, the LAANPOLE has no preset stops but gives you a continuous range. It suits people who want to adjust length freely. Run each section through its full range once in the garage and check that the locks hold when you lean on them gently. If a lock ever feels loose, stop using the pole until you have tightened or replaced it. Its bowl shape helps in wind, since fruit settles to the center instead of sliding to the rim.
products.bestFor: Soft fruit on tall trees where a curved cushion helps.
cons: No preset stops to repeat settings

products.name: ALongwujin Fruit Picker Pole, 27 to 75 Inch
products.description:
The ALongwujin is a segmented pole: interchangeable sections that connect to create 27 to 75 inches of length. The listing describes a thickened commercial-grade stainless steel shaft and a metal basket with rubber-capped claws that grip gently.

Segmented design has a charm all its own. There are no locks to slip and no telescoping tubes to jam with sap. You simply add or remove pieces. That simplicity makes it a reliable choice for casual use on small trees.

The limit is reach. At 75 inches maximum, it cannot work a tall tree, and compared with the 26 foot telescoping poles in this guide, it is a short tool. It is the right pole for a small orchard of dwarf trees or for fruit at head height. Because the pole is short, you can use it with one hand for light fruit and two hands for heavier ones. Add a section only when you have to, and keep the pieces together in a canvas bag so none go missing. It is also a pleasant pole for a first-time picker who wants to learn the motion without a tall stretch.
products.bestFor: Small trees and low fruit where simple sections beat telescoping locks.
cons: Sections must be joined by hand

products.name: Walensee 13FT Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The Walensee 13FT is a stainless steel telescoping pole from 35 to 158 inches with a cushioned foam pad. The listing describes the pole as designed to extend to reach high branches without a ladder, and as reinforced and lightweight for its class.

Steel gives the pole a rigid feel. At a mid-range length it flexes less than a thin aluminum pole, so the basket stays where you put it. That stiffness helps when the fruit is heavy and you have to hold the pole steady.

The tradeoff is that steel is heavier than aluminum at full length. If you plan to hold the pole overhead for long sessions, you may prefer an aluminum pole such as the SKGPOLE. Compared with the BlumeTrec, the Walensee telescopes rather than using sections. Use it when you want a stiff mid-range pole. It is a pole that suits people who like to feel the stiffness in their hands, because it does not bend as much as a thin tube. Rinse off salt or dew after each session to keep the finish in good shape. For heavy fruit the extra rigidity is a real asset, because the head does not droop when it loads.
products.bestFor: A stiff steel pole for mid-height trees.
cons: Heavier than aluminum at full length

products.name: BlumeTrec 6.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
products.description:
The BlumeTrec 6.5FT uses 16 inch stainless steel sections to build a pole from 35 to 77 inches. A thick foam pad lines the basket. The listing describes the pole as lightweight and durable, premium stainless steel.

Its short length is a strength for control. The pole is easy to aim, easy to store and easy to carry. A segmented pole is also free of locks, which means nothing to jam.

It will not reach a tall tree, but that is not its job. Compared with the ALongwujin, the BlumeTrec has foam padding and slightly more length. It is a good second pole for low fruit. Since each section is only 16 inches, it fits in a car trunk or a shed shelf with space to spare. Label the sections with a marker if you own more than one pole, so they never get mixed up. It pairs well with a longer pole for the same garden, so the short one handles the lower half of the tree.
products.bestFor: Low fruit where a short, lock-free pole is easiest.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Telescoping poles like the TONYINGO, SKGPOLE, LAANPOLE and Walensee extend in one motion, while sectional poles like the ALongwujin and BlumeTrec join pieces. Telescoping is faster and reaches higher, but locks can slip. Sectional is simpler and more durable but takes longer to adjust. A simple way to think about it is that sectional poles never surprise you, while telescoping poles reward you with speed. If you pick a lot of fruit across a season, speed matters.

The TONYINGO locks at 5, 9, 12, 16 and 20 feet using flip locks. Sticky sap and dew can make any lock slip. Look for locks that you can close with the heel of your hand and that click firmly into place. Test the lock with a firm downward press before each session, because a quick squeeze in the garage is far safer than finding out at full height.

Aluminum poles such as the SKGPOLE, TONYINGO and LAANPOLE are lighter. Stainless steel poles such as the Walensee, BlumeTrec and ALongwujin are stiffer. Lighter is better for overhead work. Stiffer is better for heavy fruit at short length. Think about who else will use the pole. A lighter aluminum pole is kinder to smaller or older hands, while a stiffer steel pole suits someone who wants a solid feel.

The ALongwujin reaches 75 inches, the BlumeTrec 77 inches, the Walensee 158 inches, and the 26 foot poles reach up to 20 feet of shaft. Longer poles sway and are harder to aim. Pick the shortest that works. Many gardeners find that the pole they use most is the shortest one that works. Buying taller than you need adds weight, sway and risk with little benefit.

The SKGPOLE uses a 3/4 inch American standard thread. A standard thread lets you use other heads and tools on the same pole. Check the thread if you plan to share a pole with other tools. It is also worth keeping the original packaging or a photo of the thread, so you can describe it exactly if you ever order a replacement head.

Every pole here is metal. Metal conducts electricity and can be deadly near overhead wires. Check above you before extending, and keep a safe distance. Call the utility if a branch touches a wire. If the tree is close to a house, a roof edge or a fence line, plan your standing position so that the pole never swings toward a wire.

howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how each pole changes length. The TONYINGO uses preset locks, the SKGPOLE and LAANPOLE telescope freely, and the ALongwujin and BlumeTrec use sections. This is the difference that shows up fastest in daily use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material and stiffness
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed aluminum against stainless steel. Aluminum poles scored higher for weight, and steel poles scored higher for rigidity. It mainly changes how tired your arms feel after an hour.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated reach, from 75 inches on the ALongwujin to over 26 feet on the LAANPOLE. We matched reach to typical tree heights. Reach claims are the makers' figures, so they are best used for comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Basket and thread
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked basket size and thread. The TONYINGO basket is 5.7 by 13 inches, and the SKGPOLE has a 3/4 inch thread. A larger basket helps when the fruit is big.

howWeEvaluated.description: We considered electrical risk on every pole, and flagged it clearly. Safety guidance was part of the ranking. This criterion outweighed every other one in our ranking.

faq.q: How long a pole do I need?
faq.a: Add your own height to the pole length and subtract a foot or two for handling. A 12 foot pole reaches fruit at about 16 feet. Choose the shortest that works. A tape measure and a quick look at the tree are all you need. Measure from the ground to the highest fruit you actually want, not to the top of the tree, since that is the reach you need.

They can if the lock slips. Sap and dew make locks slippery. Wipe the sections and check the lock before lifting. A few drops of silicone spray can help the sections glide. Before each lift, slide your hand along the pole to confirm every twist lock is tight, and shorten the pole if one feels loose.

faq.q: Which is lighter, aluminum or steel?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter at long length. Steel is stiffer. Both conduct electricity. Pick based on how long you will hold it. If you spend long sessions with the pole raised, a lighter aluminum model will tire your shoulders less than a stiffer steel one.

faq.q: Can I use the pole for other tasks?
faq.a: A standard 3/4 inch thread lets you fit compatible tools. Check the thread of each tool. The SKGPOLE uses the American standard. A cheap adapter may also be available. Test any new head on the pole thread by hand first, since a loose fit at full reach can drop the tool onto the ground or the fruit.

faq.q: How do I stay safe near wires?
faq.a: Look up before extending, keep well clear and never work in wet weather near lines. If a tree touches a wire, call the utility. Do not try to move the branch. Keep the tree trimmed so branches stay clear of lines. Stay several feet away from any overhead line, take the pole down in damp conditions, and ask the utility to trim branches that grow near wires.

faq.q: How do I store the pole?
faq.a: Collapse the sections and store the pole dry. Hang it on two hooks or lay it flat. Clean sap off the sections before storing. Do not store it in a damp shed. A pair of wall hooks in the garage keeps the pole off the floor, where moisture can corrode the locks over a winter.
